**Verdict:** A high-risk, high-reward turnaround that fits the high-potential sleeve — buy a small starter position sized at the low end of the sleeve budget.

**Quality read:** This is a distressed business, not a healthy one — own that up front. It designs computer processors (CPUs) and graphics chips (GPUs) but is the clear #2 against dominant rivals, and its server-chip share has collapsed to under 1%. Revenue fell 27.5% in the latest full year to $6,785M, after only 3.9% growth the year before. The company has lost money three years running, and the losses are getting bigger (-$141M, then -$685M, then -$1,122M). The balance sheet is the scariest part: total debt of $3,842M against $1,334.5M of cash, and stockholders' equity is actually NEGATIVE (-$700M) — meaning on paper the company owes more than it owns. Interest alone costs $272M a year. What keeps it alive is a floor: it makes the custom chips inside both major game consoles under long-term contracts, which brings in steady money regardless of the turnaround. A respected chip-engineer CEO took over about two years ago, cut costs hard, refinanced the debt, and bet the company on one new product: a clean-sheet CPU design claimed to run about 40% faster per clock, due in roughly 12-18 months. If it works, it is the first genuinely competitive product in a decade — and the dominant rival just showed its first manufacturing stumble in decades.

**Price read:** You cannot compute a price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) here because the company loses money, so there are no earnings to divide by. On sales, though, it is cheap: price-to-sales (P/S) is 0.43 and enterprise-value-to-sales (EV/S, which adds debt into the price) is 0.80 — low for a chip company. A precise fair-value estimate is not really possible because the value depends almost entirely on a product that does not exist yet; the console business alone roughly justifies today's price, so you are effectively getting the new CPU as a free lottery ticket. One thing to note so it doesn't mislead you: the reported gross margin (profit left after making the product) of 27% is artificially low because of one-time inventory write-downs — the underlying level is closer to 32%.

**Thesis fit:** This is exactly what the high-potential sleeve exists for — an asymmetric bet where the position is capped small (1-2% of the portfolio), so the most you can lose is limited, but the upside is a multi-fold re-rating if the turnaround lands. High volatility tolerance and a 5+ year horizon are both required, and both are present. You hold no CVM today, so this initiates a new position.

**Data quality:** Both analyst inputs are HIGH-confidence and fresh (full-year results filed ~2 weeks ago). Conviction is held to MEDIUM anyway because the outcome is binary and rests on a single unproven product plus a fragile balance sheet — not because the data is thin.

**Recommendation:** Buy a starter position at ~1% of total portfolio (the low end of the 1-2% sleeve band) given the equity deficit and thin covenant headroom; keep dry powder to add only if the product proves out. FALSIFIERS that would kill the thesis: (1) the new CPU core slips well past ~18 months or launches materially below its claimed performance / fails to win share; (2) a covenant breach or forced, heavily dilutive emergency capital raise before the product ships; (3) loss or non-renewal of the console chip contracts — that removes the floor; (4) cash burn accelerating toward the $1,334.5M cash cushion with no revenue stabilization. THE CLOCK: interim quarterly prints over the next 12-18 months are burn/stabilization checkpoints; the hard catalyst is the clean-sheet CPU launch in ~12-18 months. Honest re-rating horizon: 2-3 years, and it is genuinely hard to pin more tightly than that — that imprecision is itself a reason conviction is MEDIUM, not HIGH.

**Sources:** fundamentals/CVM, news/CVM
